13-095.r: Google Apps is not a web browser; Opera, Vivaldi and Mozilla Firefox are.

13-096.r: Web crawler = web spider (spiderbot): a bot that systematically browses the web, mainly for indexing.

13-097.r: WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access) → communication technology for long-distance wireless data.

13-098.r: All four are computer terms: analog computer, binary code (computer language), modes (real, protected, virtual real) and chip (hardware).
13-098.c: The book gives no single answer (*): every option is a computer term.

13-099.r: VIRUS → Vital Information Resources Under Siege: a malicious program that disrupts a computer and its files.

13-100.r: Computer virus → man-made software program that loads without your knowledge, runs against your wishes and replicates itself.

13-106.r: Program that infects other programs and spreads copies of itself into them → virus; viruses, worms, Trojans and bots are all malware.

13-107.r: Trojan → malware disguised as legitimate software; once installed it acts like a virus or worm but does not copy itself into other files.
13-107.t: Don't confuse: keylogger records keystrokes; ransomware encrypts data for ransom; spyware steals data.

13-108.r: Firewall (hardware, software or both) → protects private networks from unauthorised access; examines every message entering or leaving.

13-109.r: Firewall → network security device that monitors traffic and blocks unauthorised access using set security rules.

13-110.r: Michael Angelo virus → designed to infect MS-DOS on 6 March 1992; first found in Australia in 1991.

13-111.r: Stuxnet → computer worm targeting industrial control systems; found in computers of Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant (sabotaging nuclear centrifuges).

13-112.r: WannaCry (ransomware, May 2017), Petya (2016) and EternalBlue (exploit used in WannaCry) → cyberattacks.

13-113.r: Pegasus spyware → developed by Israel's NSO Group; can enter a device without the target clicking anything.

13-114.r: MS-DOS → introduced by Microsoft in August 1981; command-line OS written by Tim Paterson, derived from 86-DOS.

13-116.r: Windows 3 → released by Microsoft in 1990; Windows 11 released in October 2021.

13-119.r: UNIX → multi-user operating system developed by AT&T in 1969.

13-120.r: UNIX → operating system, widely used in servers and workplaces; Java, Oracle and MS-Office are not operating systems.

13-121.r: Core of the UNIX operating system → kernel (allocates memory and time, handles files); UNIX parts: kernel, shell, commands and applications.

13-122.r: Not true: 'GNU is not compatible with Unix' (it is upward-compatible). GNU = 'GNU's Not Unix', free software started by Richard Stallman (announced September 1983).

13-123.r: Microsoft Office → office suite (Word, Excel, PowerPoint), not an operating system; Linux, Windows and Unix are operating systems.

13-124.r: Computer memory types → semiconductor (primary), magnetic and optical (secondary); server is not a memory type.

13-125.r: Computer memory is measured in bits (binary digits, 0 or 1), the smallest unit.

13-126.r: Binary numbers → only 0 and 1 (often called low and high).

13-127.h: Write 1 under each place value you use, 0 under the rest.

13-129.r: Self-complementing code: weights must sum to 9 → 5211, 2421, 3321, 4311 are; 8421 and 5421 are not.

13-131.r: 1 byte = 8 bits (binary digits); 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB.
13-131.h: Byte = 8 bits; every step up after that is × 1024.

13-137.r: Bit = binary digit: the smallest unit of data, value 0 or 1.

13-138.r: Word length is measured in bits; 8 bits = 1 byte; 1024 bytes = 1 KB; 1024 KB = 1 MB.

13-143.r: Smallest of KB, MB, GB, TB → KB. Order: bit < byte < KB < MB < GB < TB; 1 GB = 1024 MB (not 1024 KB).

13-149.r: MB → megabyte; 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB.

13-150.r: MAC (Media Access Control) address → 48 bits; physical address at the data link layer (Layer 2), written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.

13-151.r: Unicode represents each character with 2 bytes = 16 bits.

13-152.r: Basic unit of quantum information → qubit (quantum bit), a two-state quantum system (e.g. electron spin up/down).

13-153.r: Qubit → term from quantum computing: the quantum counterpart of the classical bit.

13-154.r: Both true: .NET framework → Microsoft; Java → James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (released 1995).

13-155.r: Private network of a company at one location → LAN (Local Area Network): links computers in a limited area.

13-157.r: Ethernet → LAN protocol controlling data transmission (IEEE 802.3).

13-158.r: In a database, a field → a category of information.

13-159.r: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) → part of the CPU that does calculations and logical decisions.

13-161.r: CD → Compact Disc; IC → Integrated Circuit; IP → Internet Protocol; CAD → Computer Aided Design.

13-162.r: Magnetic tape and magnetic disk both store very large data; a disk stores more; tapes were common before hard disks.

13-163.r: Blu-ray vs DVD: Blu-ray holds HD video (DVD standard definition) and several times more data (25 GB per layer vs 4.7 GB); both 1.2 mm thick → 1 and 2.

13-164.r: Compiler → software that converts a programming language into machine code; not hardware (printer, mouse, keyboard are).

13-165.r: Assembler → software that converts basic instructions into bit patterns; not hardware (magnetic tape, printer, CRT are).

13-166.r: Excel → Microsoft software, not hardware; mouse, printer and monitor are hardware (physical parts).

13-167.r: Operating system → software, not hardware; printer, keyboard and mouse are hardware.

13-168.r: Compiler → system software (programming language to machine language); transistor and integrated circuit are hardware.

13-169.r: Internet Explorer → closed-source software; book lists Google Chrome, Linux and OpenOffice as open source.
13-169.c: Google Chrome itself is proprietary freeware built on the open-source Chromium; the answer (Internet Explorer) still stands.

13-170.r: Cloud service layers: SaaS, PaaS, IaaS; 'hardware as a service' is not an independent layer.

13-171.r: Index hole → floppy disk: marks the beginning point of stored data.

13-173.r: Program controlling a computer's basic functions → operating system (memory, device and process management).

13-174.r: Brain of the computer → CPU (Central Processing Unit), where most calculations happen.

13-175.r: Most important part of a computer → CPU (Central Processing Unit), which analyses received data.

13-178.r: Not correct: CPU = Central (not Control) Processing Unit. Correct: Email = Electronic mail; WWW = World Wide Web; ALU = Arithmetic Logic Unit.

13-179.r: Control Unit decodes program instructions and directs all operations; CPU units: Control Unit, ALU, Memory Unit.

13-180.r: Intel Core i9 → processor (high-end CPUs with 8 to 24 cores).

13-181.r: Word processing software: Page-Maker, WordStar, MS-Word → all; MS-Word is application software.

13-183.r: MS Word → processing text data (creating and publishing printable text).

13-184.r: Word processing, spreadsheets and photo editing → application software (also CAD, desktop publishing, audio/video editing).

13-186.r: Basic unit of an Excel spreadsheet where data is entered → cell (meeting of a row and a column).

13-187.r: E-mail application (email client) → Microsoft Outlook; others: Mozilla Thunderbird, Apple Mail.

13-188.r: Adobe Photoshop → raster graphics editor; book gives two answers: graphics software and multimedia software.

13-189.r: A Word document, video or MP3 → a file; the extension shows its type (.doc → Word, .mp3 → music).

13-191.r: MPEG → Moving Picture Experts Group (ISO/IEC working group for audio-video compression standards).

13-192.r: Second-generation computers → transistors (first generation → vacuum tubes).

13-193.r: Third-generation computers → integrated circuits (ICs), invented by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce.

13-194.r: Miniaturisation of computers → integrated circuit chips (invented 1958), made of semiconductor, normally silicon.

13-196.r: IC chips are made of silicon (a semiconductor); J.S. Kilby built the first complete IC chip in 1958.
